title: Rotational Partition Functions of Diatomic Gases Contain a Symmetry Number
lead: The rotational partition function of a diatomic gas is a sum over the rigid rotor's levels, which can be taken as an integral when the levels lie close together. A homonuclear molecule needs one more factor, the symmetry number.
notes: Adapted from B. L. Tembe's lecture notes (IIT Bombay, www.chem.iitb.ac.in/~bltembe/pdfs/ch_3.pdf), shared under the book's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
exercise_notes: The book prints no exercises for this section; the one here is new and AI-written, its answers checked by computation, with its Bloom level and concept tags chosen by AI.

exercises.source_id: What is the rotational partition function of $H_2$ at 300 K?
exercises.prompt: Use Table 1 to find the rotational partition function at 300 K of (a) $\mathrm{N_2}$ and (b) $\mathrm{HCl}$.

answer.solution: Both rotational temperatures are far below 300 K, so $\kqrot = \kT/\kThetarot σ$ (Equation 18.6.6) holds. (a) $\mathrm{N_2}$ has two identical ends, $σ = 2$: $\kqrot = 300/(2.88 \times 2) = 52.1$. (b) $\mathrm{HCl}$ has $σ = 1$: $\kqrot = 300/15.2 = 19.7$. The heavier, longer nitrogen molecule has more closely spaced levels, and even after halving for its symmetry it has more of them within reach.

footnotes.html: The denominator is $8\pi^2 I$: $E_J = J(J+1)h^2/8\pi^2 I$.

derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 18.6 Rotational Partition Functions of Diatomic Gases Contain a Symmetry Number

assumes.text: When the levels lie close together beside $k\kT$, the sum over $J$ can be replaced by an integral over $J$.

steps.cap: Substitute $x = J(J+1)$, so $dx = (2J+1)\,dJ$, and $x$ runs from $0$ to $\infty$ as $J$ does.

nodes.note: The book prints the integrand's exponential as $R^{-\tilde{B}J(J+1)/kT}$ and the result as $kT/\tilde{B}$, with $kT$ in wavenumbers as Example 18.6.1 takes it; in energy units the result is $kT/hc\tilde{B}$.
